UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                       BEFORE THE
                         FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                                 )                      Docket No. ER26-1088-000

                               MOTION FOR LEAVE AND ANSWER OF
                            CONSTELLATION ENERGY GENERATION, LLC

            Constellation1 moves for leave and submits this answer in response to the Transmission

Owners’ request that the Commission grant rehearing, or in the alternative, clarification2 of its

Thirty-Day Compliance Order.3 The Transmission Owners ask that the Commission “permit PJM

to define Co-Located Load based on the Point of Change in Ownership.”4 They claim “the Point

of Change in Ownership is the more appropriate demarcation”5 and that “PJM was not proposing

a stylistic change” but identified “a substantive problem with using ‘Point of Interconnection’ as

the operative boundary in the definition of Co-Located Load”6 as required by the PJM Co-Location

 Order. The Transmission Owners argue that the Commission “did not meaningfully engage with

PJM’s explanation”7 in the Thirty-Day Compliance Order.

            “Substantive problem[s]”8 with a Commission order must be raised on rehearing of that

order, not on compliance or rehearing of a compliance order. The Commission should deny the

Transmission Owners’ requests because they seek the untimely rehearing of the PJM Co-Location

Order, incorrectly argue that the Commission violated the Administrative Procedure Act, and seek

to constrain the new transmission services or impose burdensome technical requirements.

Constellation’s proposal to add to the “Conditions Precedent for Receiving Service” should

address any of the Transmission Owners’ concerns regarding load opportunistically locating in

such a way as to claim Co-Located Load status and services.9

I.          The Commission Should Reject the Transmission Owners’ Untimely Request for
            Rehearing

            The Transmission Owners’ Rehearing and Clarification Request is categorically an

untimely, statutorily barred request for rehearing of the PJM Co-Location Order.10 The Rehearing

and Clarification Request challenges the use of Point of Interconnection in the definition of Co-

Located Load adopted by the PJM Co-Location Order. The Transmission Owners argue the

Commission should “permit PJM to define Co-Located Load based on the Point of Change in

 Ownership” instead of the Point of Interconnection.11 They argue that the “simplest and most

straightforward solution is for the Commission to grant rehearing and permit PJM to use ‘Point of

Change in Ownership’” instead of Point of Interconnection “in the definition of Co-Located

Load.”12 The Transmission Owners claim using Point of Interconnection to define Co-Located

Load “may create confusion regarding where protection is required”13 and “could invite entities to

exploit certain interconnection configurations in order to expand the availability of the new

transmission services beyond the scope the Commission intended in the December 18 Order.”14

            The Transmission Owners’ claims are too late. Like PJM, the Transmission Owners failed

to timely seek rehearing of the PJM Co-Location Order on the use of Point of Interconnection in

the Commission-mandated definition of Co-Located Load.15 The Federal Power Act requires

petitions for rehearing of a Commission order to be filed within 30 days of that order’s issuance.

The Commission “has no discretion to extend that deadline.”16

II.         The Commission Should Reject Claims that it Failed to Meaningfully Consider PJM’s
            Explanation for Proposing a Non-Compliant Definition of Co-Located Load

            The Transmission Owners argue that the Thirty-Day Compliance Order “did not

meaningfully address PJM’s explanation” for changing the Commission-mandated “Point of

 Interconnection” in the definition of Co-Located Load to a new “Point of Change in Ownership.”17

However, the Commission found that PJM’s non-compliant definition was an untimely rehearing

request and outside the scope of compliance.18 The Commission is not required to address

procedurally improper arguments that are collateral attacks on an initial order and outside the scope

of a compliance proceeding.19

            And even if the Commission were required to consider PJM’s arguments, it clearly did so

and engaged in reasoned decision-making in rendering its decision. For example, the Commission

found that “PJM fail[ed] to demonstrate why Point of Change in Ownership is consistent with the

Commission’s directive in the PJM Co-Location Order that PJM adopt the definition of Co-

Located Load specified therein [and that] the record here suggests PJM’s proposed modification

to this definition may lead to uncertainty or delays for parties in Co-Located Load

configurations.”20 Thus, the Commission considered the record before it and, based on that

     rehearing.”); NorthWestern Corp., 113 FERC ¶ 61,215 at P 9 (“The Commission has long established that
     compliance filings must be limited to the specific directives ordered by the Commission.”); Cal. Power Exch. Corp.,
     101 FERC ¶ 61,330, at P 25 (2002) (“The purpose of a compliance filing is to make only the revisions directed by
     the Commission.”).

 evidence, rejected PJM’s effort to change the definition of Co-Located Load specifically to avoid

the “uncertainty or delays” it would create.21

III.        The Commission Should Reject Transmission Owners’ Attempt to Limit Access to New
            Services

            The Transmission Owners claim defining Co-Located Load at the Point of Interconnection

will let potential customers “stretch the definition of Co-Located Load,”22 engage in

“gamesmanship”23 and “manipulat[ion],”24 and expand “the new transmission services beyond

their intended scope … to the detriment of efficiency and reliability.”25 These arguments are

further examples of the Transmission Owners seeking to constrain access to new transmission

services to make them virtually impossible to ever utilize.26

             Indeed, the Transmission Owners specifically request that the Commission “limit” co-

location arrangements to “arrangements involving generation and load that are meaningfully co-

located.”27 Despite the imprecision of the term, at the very least the Transmission Owners intend

“meaningfully co-located” to mean where the load and generator are “truly located at the same

site” and the load does not “rely” on the Transmission Owner-owned facility to “qualify” as Co-

Located Load28—that is, a Transmission Owner-owned facility is not located between the load and

the generating facility. In other words, the load and generating facility are located on the customer

side of the Point of Change in Ownership29—the exact condition that the Thirty-Day Compliance

Order rejected.30

            The PJM Co-Location Order does not require load and a generating facility to be located

“at the same site.”31 An “end-use customer load” must only be “physically connected to the

     with its generators at certain facilities due to Exelon’s concerns that such requests are not allowed under the Tariff
     without arranging for wholesale transmission or retail distribution service.”).

 facilities of an existing or planned Customer Facility on the Interconnection Customer’s side of

the Point of Interconnection to the PJM Transmission System.”32 The distance between the load

and the generation facility has no relevance and varies across interconnections. This is because a

generator must deliver energy at the Point of Interconnection.33

            The location of the Point of Change in Ownership does not affect the physical connection

of the load and the generator or the design requirements determined necessary to maintain system

reliability. The “Point of Change in Ownership” means “the point, as set forth Schedule B of the

Generation Interconnection Agreement, where the Project Developer’s Interconnection Facilities

connect to the Transmission Owner’s Interconnection Facilities.”34 It is a point negotiated by the

Interconnection Customer and Transmission Owner to establish operation, maintenance and

ownership responsibilities over the life of the interconnection and can differ from one

interconnection to the next. The design of the interconnection facilities, including the fault clearing

design, are not made more complex by the location of the Point of Change in Ownership as the

Transmission Owners imply.35

IV.         The Commission Should Deny the Transmission Owners’ Unnecessary Clarifications

            The Transmission Owners claim two clarifications are “necessary” for the Commission to

“rel[y] on the ‘Point of Interconnection’ for purposes of eligibility for the new transmission

 Services”36: first, that the “use of ‘Point of Interconnection’ in the definition of Co-Located Load

does not dilute or undermine the parties’ obligations with respect to Protection Systems,”37 and

second, that “Transmission-Owner-owned facilities on the Customer Side of the Interconnection

are not part of Co-Located Load arrangement”38 and related clarifications to address

“gamesmanship by customers taking advantage of Co-Located Load arrangements.”39

            The Commission should dismiss the Transmission Owners’ requests. There is no need for

the Commission to clarify the parties’ obligations related to protection systems.40 The parties’

obligations are already set forth in the Illustrative Tariff.41

            The Commission does not need to clarify that Transmission Owner-owned facilities are

not part of the Co-Located Load arrangement given “the reliability impacts of significant amounts

of ‘behind the meter’ load.”42 Co-Located Load and behind the meter load are not the same.

Moreover, clarifying “that Transmission Owner-owned facilities are not part of the Co-Location

 arrangement”43 raises the same uncertainty and delay concerns as raised by PJM’s non-compliant

definition of Co-Located Load.44 If the existence of a Transmission Owner-owned facility located

between the load and the generating facility is allowed to break the required “physical connection,”

certain load arrangements could no longer qualify as Co-Located Load. This concern is not merely

hypothetical. Generators do not have sole control over the configuration and ownership of

interconnection facilities and instead are subject to Transmission Owner and PJM interconnection

specifications, with any attempt to dispute Transmission Owner requirements resulting in an

interconnection delay.

           There is also no need for the Commission to “clarify that customers may not rely on …

other third-party owned facilities with which the customer has no contractual arrangement, to

satisfy the definition of Co-Located Load.”45 Instead, the Commission should simply adopt

Constellation’s earlier recommendation to add to the “Conditions Precedent for Receiving

Service” the requirement that the Eligible Customer identify the Customer Facilities in the Co-

Location Arrangement and if the Customer Facilities include an existing generator, require

certification that the existing generator supports the request.46

           Lastly, the Commission can dismiss the Transmission Owners’ request that the

Commission clarify that “if a customer meets the definition of Co-Located Load based on the

location of the Point of Interconnection, that customer must separately meet the definition of

the “Eligible Customer will be the party responsible for executing a transmission service

agreement.”49 No clarification is needed.

                                                  CONCLUSION

           For the foregoing reasons, the Commission should accept this answer intended to support

the Commission’s decision-making, deny the Transmission Owners’ Rehearing and Clarification

Request, and affirm the Commission’s Thirty-Day Compliance Order rejecting PJM’s non-

compliant definition of Co-Located Load.
